items.title: Lesson 2 "Explain" (Figure 7): An electroscope has been given a positive charge, so its leaves are spread apart. A negatively charged rod is then touched to the knob. What happens to the leaves?

body.html: The electroscope starts with a deficiency of electrons (positive). The rod has an excess of electrons (negative) and actually touches the knob.
Touching transfers charge (conduction). Electrons move from the negative rod onto the positive electroscope.

The electroscope gains electrons, so its net positive charge shrinks and the leaves move closer together. If the rod supplies more electrons than are needed to neutralize it, the electroscope passes through neutral (leaves hang down) and ends up negative, so the leaves spread apart again.

answer.html: The leaves first fall together as electrons flow onto the electroscope; if the rod has enough excess electrons, they fall completely and then spread apart again as the electroscope becomes negatively charged.

items.title: Lesson 2 "CCC: Cause and Effect" (grounding and a power surge): A tanker truck is delivering fuel. A grounding cable is clamped from the truck's metal frame to the earth before the hose is connected. Make a cause-and-effect table showing how grounding keeps the process safe.

body.html: Fuel flowing through the hose rubs on the pipe and the truck body and separates charge. A conductor connected to Earth lets excess charge flow away, because Earth can absorb large amounts of charge without a noticeable change.

Cause: charge builds up on the truck as fuel flows Effect with grounding Effect without grounding Friction of fuel in the hose leaves excess charge on the truck frame Charge flows through the cable into Earth, so the frame stays near 0 V Charge stays on the frame, which rises to a high voltage A worker touches the truck or the nozzle touches the tank No difference in potential between them, so no spark A large potential difference can make a spark across the gap Fuel vapor is present near the connection No spark, so no ignition A spark can ignite the vapor and cause a fire

answer.html: With the buildup of charge as the cause, grounding gives the charge a path into Earth so the truck stays at the same potential as its surroundings; without grounding the charge can build up and make a dangerous spark.

items.title: 15 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): Two charged balloons hang apart in a room without touching. State Coulomb's law and explain how it lets you predict the force one exerts on the other.

body.html: Coulomb's law says the magnitude of the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: 𝐹= 𝐾𝑞<sub>𝐴</sub>𝑞<sub>𝐵</sub>/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup>. Measuring the balloons' charges and the distance between their centers lets you compute the size of the force. The charge signs give the direction (like repel, unlike attract). The force acts across the gap even though the balloons do not touch.

answer.html: 𝐹= 𝐾𝑞<sub>𝐴</sub>𝑞<sub>𝐵</sub>/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, knowing the charges and the separation gives the size of the force, and the signs show whether the balloons attract or repel.

answer.html: The force becomes 1.5 times as large. For like charges the force is repulsive; for opposite charges it is attractive.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): In charging an electroscope by induction with a positive rod, what happens if the rod is moved away before the ground connection is removed?

body.html: In induction with grounding, the rod's field pulls electrons from the ground onto the electroscope. If the rod is removed while the ground connection remains, nothing holds those extra electrons there.

A positive rod near the knob attracts electrons from the ground onto the electroscope. When the rod is moved away with the ground still attached, the electrons are no longer attracted and flow back to the ground, so the electroscope returns to neutral.

answer.html: The electroscope does not stay charged: the extra electrons flow back to the ground and it returns to neutral.

items.title: 19 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): A student adds more charge to a charged electroscope. Predict what happens to the angle of the leaves and explain it with forces.

body.html: Equilibrium of torques. Each leaf is acted on by gravity (down) and by the repulsion from the other leaf (outward).

Adding charge increases the repulsion, since 𝐹∝𝑞<sub>1</sub>𝑞<sub>2</sub>. At the old angle the outward torque now exceeds the torque due to gravity, so the leaves swing farther apart. As they spread, the repulsion decreases (the leaves get farther apart) and gravity's torque grows, until the two balance at a larger angle.

answer.html: The leaves spread to a larger angle, stopping where the outward electrostatic repulsion again balances the downward pull of gravity.

items.title: 20 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): A small neutral piece of aluminum foil is attracted to a charged comb, but after touching the comb it is suddenly pushed away. What properties of charge explain both observations?

body.html: Before touching: the foil is neutral and the comb's field separates its charge. The nearer, oppositely charged side is attracted more strongly than the farther side is repelled, because force is stronger at shorter distances. After touching: some of the comb's charge flows onto the foil (a conductor), so the foil now has the same sign of charge as the comb, and like charges repel.

answer.html: A neutral object contains both kinds of charge, which can separate, so the nearer opposite charge makes the net force attractive. After contact the foil takes on charge of the comb's sign, and like charges repel.

items.title: 21 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): How can you charge an electroscope negatively using (a) a negative rod, (b) a positive rod?

question.html: Work (a): Touch the negative rod to the knob (conduction): electrons flow from the rod onto the electroscope, leaving it negative. Work (b): Use induction with grounding. Bring the positive rod near (not touching) the knob; touch the knob with a finger so electrons flow from ground onto the electroscope; remove the finger first, then remove the rod. The electroscope is left with an excess of electrons.

answer.html: (a) Touch the negative rod to the knob. (b) Bring the positive rod near the knob, ground the knob briefly, remove the ground, then remove the rod.

items.title: 23 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2): A small positive plastic sphere is brought close to a large negatively charged metal sphere. Why is the measured force larger than

question.html: 1 / 𝑟2 predicts (with 𝑟 measured between centers) when the spheres are close?

body.html: Coulomb's law with 𝑟 measured between centers is valid only if each charge is spread uniformly over a sphere. Free charge on a conductor moves.

The positive plastic sphere attracts the negative charge on the metal sphere, pulling it toward the near side. The metal sphere's charge is no longer centered, so the effective charge is closer than the center-to-center distance, and the force is larger than expected.

answer.html: Charge on the metal sphere is pulled toward the near side when the plastic sphere approaches, so the charge distribution is no longer centered and the actual force is greater than Coulomb's law (using center-to-center distance) predicts.

The electroscope loses electrons, so its net negative charge shrinks and the leaves fall closer together. If the rod's positive charge is large enough, the electroscope can pass through neutral (leaves hang down) and end up positive, so the leaves would spread apart again.

answer.html: The leaves would fall together as the electroscope loses electrons to the rod; if the rod has enough positive charge, the leaves would fall completely and then spread apart again as the electroscope becomes positively charged.

items.title: Lesson 2 "CCC: Cause and Effect" (grounding and a power surge) Question: How does grounding keep a home safe in a power surge? Make a table of cause and effect.

body.html: Excess charge from a surge moves along conductors toward lower potential; Earth can absorb large amounts of charge without a noticeable change.

Cause: power surge (extra charge/voltage on the wiring) Effect with grounding Effect without grounding Excess charge enters the wiring or an appliance's metal case Charge flows through the ground wire into Earth, so the case stays near 0 V Charge stays on the case, which can be at a high voltage A person touches the appliance Little or no potential difference between person and case, so no shock Large potential difference, so charge flows through the person (shock) Charge builds up in the circuit A fuse or breaker can trip when large current flows to ground Damage to electronics or fire is more likely

answer.html: With the surge as the cause, grounding provides a path so the excess charge flows safely into Earth; without grounding the charge stays on the appliance and may pass through a person or damage equipment.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: In an electroscope being charged by induction, what happens if the charging rod is moved away

body.html: In induction by grounding, the rod's field pushes electrons off (or onto) the electroscope through the ground connection. If the rod is removed while the ground connection remains, nothing holds those electrons in the new arrangement.
Suppose a negative rod pushed electrons from the electroscope into the ground. When the rod is moved away, electrons flow back from the ground to the electroscope, restoring its neutrality.

answer.html: The electroscope does not stay charged: charge flows back through the ground connection and the electroscope returns to neutral.

items.title: 19 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: Why do the leaves of a charged electroscope rise to a certain angle and no farther?

body.html: Equilibrium of torques. Each leaf is acted on by gravity (pulling it down) and the electrostatic repulsion from the other leaf (pushing it outward).

As the leaves spread, they are farther apart, so the repulsion decreases (1 / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>), while the gravitational torque tending to bring each leaf back down increases as it moves toward horizontal. At some angle the torques balance.

answer.html: The leaves stop rising when the outward electrostatic repulsion balances the downward pull of gravity on the leaves; moving farther apart weakens the repulsion.

items.title: 20 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: What properties explain how both positive and negative objects attract neutral objects?

body.html: A neutral object contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge, and the charges can separate (electrons move in a conductor; molecules shift or turn in an insulator). A charged object attracts the opposite charge in the neutral object and repels the same sign. Since the opposite charge is nearer, and the force is stronger at shorter distances, the attraction wins.

answer.html: Neutral objects contain both kinds of charge that can be separated, and the electrostatic force is stronger at shorter distance, so the nearer, oppositely charged side is attracted more strongly than the farther side is repelled, whichever sign the charged object has.

items.title: 21 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: How can you charge an electroscope positively using (a) a positive rod, (b) a negative rod?

question.html: Work (a): Touch the positive rod to the knob (conduction): electrons flow from the electroscope to the rod, leaving the electroscope positive. Work (b): Use induction with grounding. Bring the negative rod near (not touching) the knob; touch the knob with a finger so electrons are pushed to ground; remove the finger first, then remove the rod. The electroscope is left with a deficit of electrons.

answer.html: (a) Touch the positive rod to the knob. (b) Bring the negative rod near the knob, ground the knob briefly, remove the ground, then remove the rod.

items.title: 22 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: Spheres A (+3 𝜇C) and B (+9 𝜇C) are a distance 𝑟 apart (Figure 14). Compare the force of A

question.html: on B with that of B on A.

body.html: Newton's third law; also in Coulomb's law the product 𝑞<sub>𝐴</sub>𝑞<sub>𝐵</sub> is symmetric.
Both forces have magnitude 𝐾(3 𝜇C)(9 𝜇C) / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>. They act in opposite directions: each sphere is pushed away from the other.

answer.html: The forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, even though B has three times the charge of A.

items.title: 23 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 2) Question: Testing Coulomb's law with a small, positive plastic sphere and a large, positive metal sphere,

question.html: why is the force smaller than 1 / 𝑟<sup>2</sup> predicts when the spheres are close?

body.html: Coulomb's law with 𝑟 measured between centers is valid only if each charge is spread uniformly over a sphere. Free charge on a conductor moves.

The positive plastic sphere repels the positive charge on the metal sphere, pushing it to the far side. The metal sphere's charge is no longer centered, so the effective charge is farther away than the center-to-center distance, and the force is smaller than expected.

answer.html: Charge on the metal sphere is repelled to its far side when the plastic sphere approaches, so the charge distribution is no longer centered and the actual force is less than Coulomb's law (using center-to-center distance) predicts.
